summary: Defines the Extended Sequence Number TLV to protect IS-IS packets from replay attacks, where an attacker re-sends old but validly signed messages.

plainLanguage.summary: A running count on each message so a thief cannot replay an old one.

questions: what is the is-is extended sequence number tlv
how does is-is prevent replay attacks
subtitle: A small counter added to IS-IS hellos and sequence number packets so captured packets cannot be replayed.

tldr.problem: A replayed IS-IS packet can bounce adjacencies, cause blackholing or even some forms of denial of service. Cryptographic authentication alone does not stop an attacker from re-sending an old, validly signed packet.
tldr.mechanism: The Extended Sequence Number (ESN) TLV carries a 64-bit session number and a 32-bit packet number in IIH and SNP PDUs. A receiver accepts a PDU only if the combined 96-bit value is greater than the last one seen from that originator for that PDU type.
tldr.outcome: Replays of hellos and sequence number packets are rejected, and the TLV can be rolled out gradually with separate send and verify modes.

today: RFC 7602 is a Proposed Standard published in July 2015, and the unit metadata shows no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It remains the definition of the IS-IS ESN TLV, meant to be used alongside RFC 5304 or RFC 5310 authentication.

sections.title: The Replay Problem in IS-IS
sections.content:
IS-IS is used widely in routing and switching deployments, including data centers. A replayed IS-IS PDU can cause bouncing adjacencies, blackholing, and some forms of Denial-of-Service attacks.

At the time of writing there is no mechanism to protect IS-IS Hello (IIH) PDUs and Sequence Number PDUs (SNPs) from replay. Link State PDUs (LSPs) already have a sequence number in the LSP header, which mitigates intra-session replay, but they remain open to inter-session replay.

This RFC defines the Extended Sequence Number (ESN) TLV to close that gap. It can be deployed together with the authentication in RFC 5304 and RFC 5310. The authors note that a group key management protocol with frequent key changes could also limit replays, but none exists for IS-IS, and manually keyed systems will likely coexist with it anyway.
sections.plainLanguage: Someone could copy a real message and send it again later to cause trouble. This RFC adds a counter so copies are spotted.

sections.title: How Replays Hurt Each PDU Type
sections.content:
Securing a packet with authentication alone cannot fully stop replay. The effect depends on the PDU type.

  • IIHs: a replayed hello, such as one with an empty neighbor list (TLV 6) sent when an adjacency comes up, can make all ISs on a broadcast network bounce the adjacency. Replay can only be mitigated when authentication information is present.
  • LSPs: normal operation of the IS-IS update process recovers from LSP replay in good time, so the ESN TLV is prohibited in LSPs.
  • SNPs: a replayed CSNP can trigger unnecessary PSNPs, and a replayed CSNP or PSNP can cause unnecessary LSP flooding on the link.
sections.plainLanguage: A replayed hello is like someone yelling 'new kid here!' again and again, so everyone keeps restarting their introductions.

sections.title: The ESN TLV
sections.content:
The TLV has a 1-octet Type, a 1-octet Length and a 12-byte Value. The type code is 11 and the length is 12. The value holds a 64-bit Extended Session Sequence Number (ESSN), followed by a 32-bit, monotonically increasing, per-packet sequence number.

The TLV is optional and is defined only for IIH and SNP PDUs. IANA assigned code 11 in the IS-IS TLV Codepoints registry, marked yes for IIH and SNP and no for LSP and Purge. A PDU with more than one ESN TLV is invalid and MUST be discarded.

The ESSN MUST be nonzero. How it is encoded is a local matter. For each PDU with the TLV, the 96-bit value formed by the ESSN (the high-order 64 bits) and the packet number MUST be greater than the most recently received value in a PDU of the same type from the same IS.
sections.plainLanguage: The tag has two numbers: a big one for the whole session and a small one that counts each message. Together they only ever go up.

sections.title: Checking and Wrapping the Counter
sections.content:
If the 32-bit packet number wraps, or the router does a cold restart, the 64-bit ESSN MUST be set higher than its previous value. That keeps the combined 96-bit value moving upward.

State is kept per PDU type, per originator and per link. For IIHs the ESN information is maintained for each type of IIH PDU sent on a circuit. For SNPs, separate CSNP and PSNP information is kept. Level information is included in the PDU type. When a PDU with the TLV is accepted, the stored value for that originator and PDU type MUST be updated to the latest one received.
sections.plainLanguage: If the small counter runs out or the machine reboots, the big number is bumped up, so new messages are still bigger than every old one.

sections.title: Gradual Deployment: Send and Verify
sections.content:
The TLV can be deployed without a flag day, on some links or on the whole network. Implementations SHOULD allow configuration at each IS-IS link level, and separate control of send mode (include the TLV in your own PDUs) and verify mode (process the TLV in received PDUs).

To turn it on, first put every router on an interface in send mode, then enable verify mode on each. Once verify mode is set on an interface, all IIHs and SNPs sent on it MUST contain the TLV, and any such PDU received without it MUST be discarded. To turn it off safely, disable verify on all ISs first, then send.

If verify mode is enabled late on some nodes during an active attack, replayed PDUs can be accepted there and the network can have inconsistent views. Operators SHOULD provision verify mode in a timely fashion.
sections.plainLanguage: First everyone starts handing out numbered tickets. Only after all are doing it does anyone start refusing tickets without numbers.

sections.title: Keeping the ESSN Increasing
sections.content:
The ESSN must keep increasing for the deployed life of the node, including across cold restarts. The appendix gives two ways, and any method that keeps the property is allowed.

  • Timestamps: encode the ESSN as system time in a 64-bit unsigned value, possibly like the NTP long format. The implementation MUST NOT fall back to an old or default time after a cold restart, so system time must be preserved, for example with a battery-backed real-time clock.
  • Non-volatile storage: use the ESSN as a wrap or boot count, incremented whenever the node loses its sequence number state. If the storage is lost, keys MUST be changed to prevent replay.

Appendix B adds that because state is kept per PDU type, originator and link, a packet number skip seen in an IIH can help correlate adjacency state changes.
sections.plainLanguage: The big number can come from a clock that never goes backward, or from a notebook that counts reboots. Either way it must never go down.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The mechanism addresses the replay threat discussed in RFC 5304 and RFC 5310. It cannot stop an adversary who simply does not forward packets or who delays messages, as described in Section 3.3 of RFC 6862. Some threats in the KARP IS-IS security analysis draft are also not covered.

The RFC states that it introduces no new security concerns to IS-IS or the specifications it references.
sections.plainLanguage: The numbered tickets catch repeated messages, but they cannot catch a thief who blocks mail or just makes it late.
